stories.title: The Roof Garden
paragraphs: Priya lived with her grandpa on the top floor of a tall apartment building. There was no yard, but there was a flat roof with a sunny corner. One spring morning, Grandpa carried six clay pots up the stairs. "Today we start a garden," he said with a wink.

Priya filled each pot with dark soil. She pressed tiny tomato seeds into the dirt and gave them a drink of water. Every day after school, she climbed up to check on them. After one week, small green sprouts poked out of the soil. Priya cheered so loudly that Grandpa came up to see what was wrong.

The next morning, three of the pots were empty. Only a few torn leaves were left. A gray pigeon sat on the edge of the roof and puffed out its chest. Priya frowned at the bird. Then she ran down the stairs to tell Grandpa.

Grandpa thought for a moment. Then he pulled an old badminton net out of the hall closet. Together they stretched it over the pots and tied it to a chair. The pigeon walked around the net and pecked at it, but it could not get in. Priya planted new seeds in the empty pots.

By the end of summer, the plants were taller than Priya. They were heavy with red tomatoes. Priya picked a big basket full. She and Grandpa knocked on doors and gave tomatoes to everyone on their floor. "Next year," said Mrs. Lee from across the hall, "I want to help with the garden."

stories.title: The Missing Library Book
paragraphs: Leo's library book was due on Friday. It was a book about sharks, and he had already read it three times because he loved the photographs. On Thursday night, he went to put it in his backpack, but the book was not on his shelf.

Leo looked under his bed, where he found two dusty socks and a toy car, but no book. He searched the kitchen and checked behind the couch cushions. He even looked in the bathtub. "Mom, have you seen my shark book?" he called. Mom shook her head. "Where did you have it last?" she asked.

Leo thought hard about the last time he had held it. He remembered reading it on the front porch on Sunday afternoon, so he hurried outside. The porch was empty. Now he was starting to worry. What would he tell Ms. Brooks, the librarian?

When Leo went back inside, he heard a small voice coming from his sister's room. He peeked through the door. Nina was four years old. She sat on the floor with her stuffed animals in a circle around her. She was holding his shark book open and pointing at the pictures. "This shark has very big teeth," she told a teddy bear. "Do not worry. He lives far away in the ocean."

Leo laughed. Nina could not read yet, but she was telling the story her own way. "Can I have my book back?" he asked. Nina's face fell. Then Leo had an idea. "Tomorrow we can go to the library together," he said. "You can pick out a book of your own." Nina clapped her hands and gave him the book.

stories.title: Busy Builders
paragraphs: Beavers are some of the best builders in nature. These furry animals live in streams and ponds in many parts of North America. A beaver has a wide, flat tail and strong front teeth that never stop growing. Its back feet are webbed, like a duck's feet. They help it swim fast.

Beavers build dams across streams. First, they chew through small trees with their sharp teeth. Then they drag the logs and branches into the water. They pile up sticks, rocks, and mud until the water is blocked. Slowly, the water behind the dam fills up and becomes a deep, quiet pond.

Out in the pond, beavers often build a home called a lodge. A lodge looks like a big pile of sticks, but inside there is a dry room above the water. The doors to the lodge are under the water. Beavers can swim in and out, but most other animals cannot.

Beavers help other living things, too. The ponds they make become homes for fish, frogs, ducks, and bugs. When beavers leave an old pond, the mud at the bottom turns into rich soil, and new plants grow there. A beaver may be small, but its work can change a whole valley.

stories.title: The Fun Run
paragraphs: Every spring, Hill Street School has a fun run. Kids race two times around the big field while their families cheer. This year, Rosa wanted to win more than anything. She had practiced every evening for a month. Her best friend, Ava, was running too.

On the day of the race, the sun was bright and warm. Coach Dean blew his whistle, and everyone took off. Rosa ran fast. By the end of the first lap, she was in the lead. She could hear her dad shouting her name.

Halfway through the second lap, Rosa's shoelace came loose. Her foot caught on it, and she fell down on the grass. Her knee stung, and her eyes filled with tears. One runner passed her, then another, then three more.

Then Ava stopped beside her. "Are you okay?" Ava asked, and she held out her hand. Rosa nodded and wiped her eyes. Ava waited while Rosa tied her shoe in a double knot. Then the two girls ran the rest of the way side by side.

They crossed the finish line together, near the back of the group. Rosa did not get a ribbon this year. But when Ava's mom took a picture of the two friends, Rosa had the biggest smile of anyone on the field.

stories.title: The Picnic Mystery
paragraphs: On Saturday, the Okafor family had a picnic in the park. Dad spread a blue blanket on the grass near a big oak tree. Chidi opened the basket and took out the food. There were apples, cheese, a jug of lemonade, and four sandwiches wrapped in paper. Their dog, Biscuit, lay in the grass and watched every move.

Before lunch, the whole family walked over to the playground. Chidi and his little brother, Emeka, took turns on the slide while Mom and Dad pushed the swings. Biscuit stayed behind, resting in the shade of the oak. When they came back, Chidi counted the sandwiches. There were only three. "Someone took a sandwich!" he said.

Chidi decided to be a detective. He looked closely at the blanket. There were crumbs near the corner, and a piece of paper was torn into strips. Next to the blanket, he saw paw prints in a patch of soft dirt. They pointed toward the oak tree.

Chidi followed the prints. Behind the tree, Biscuit was lying very still with his head on his paws. He would not look at Chidi. A little bit of bread was stuck to his whiskers, and his tail gave one slow, small wag.

Dad started to laugh. "I think we found our thief," he said. Mom cut one sandwich in half so that everyone had enough to eat. Biscuit got a dog treat instead. From then on, the Okafors always kept the picnic basket closed.

stories.title: The New Girl
paragraphs: Hana's family moved to Maple Grove in the middle of the school year. On her first day, her teacher, Mr. Ruiz, gave her a desk by the window. Hana said hello in a quiet voice and looked down at her shoes. At recess, the other kids ran off in groups. Hana sat on a bench by herself and took out her sketchbook.

She began to draw a cat wearing a superhero cape. The cat had a tiny mask and a big, brave grin. Soon a boy from her class stopped beside the bench. His name was Marcus. "Whoa," he said. "Did you just make that up?" Hana nodded.

Marcus sat down next to her. He told her that he loved to write stories, but his drawings always looked like potatoes. Hana laughed for the first time all day. "Maybe you could write the words," she said, "and I could draw the pictures."

For the rest of the week, they spent every recess on the bench. Marcus wrote about Captain Whiskers, a cat who rescued lost kittens. Hana drew each part in neat little boxes. On Friday, they shared the comic with the class. Everyone wanted to know what Captain Whiskers would do next.
That afternoon, Hana's mom asked how school was going. Hana grinned. "I think I'm going to like it here," she said.

stories.title: The Lemonade Stand
paragraphs: On the first hot day of summer, Noah and Nia set up a lemonade stand. Their street was quiet, with tall trees and only a few houses. The twins made a sign that said "Cold Lemonade, 50 Cents." They filled a big jug with lemonade and ice. Then they sat down and waited.

An hour went by. A mail truck rolled past without stopping. A cat walked across the road and lay down in the shade. Only one person bought a cup, and that was their neighbor, Mrs. Kim. The ice in the jug was melting, and Nia's smile was melting too.

"Nobody comes down this street," Noah said with a sigh. Nia looked toward the end of the block. Past the corner was the park, where a soccer game was going on. She could hear kids shouting and a whistle blowing. Suddenly she jumped up. "I have an idea!"

Dad helped them carry the table, the sign and a fresh jug of lemonade to the edge of the soccer field. When the game stopped for a break, red-faced players ran toward them, waving their money. Parents lined up too. In twenty minutes, the jug was empty.
That night, the twins counted their coins on the kitchen table. They had made eleven dollars. "Next time," said Noah, "we'll start at the park."

stories.title: The Snowy Sidewalk
paragraphs: The snow fell all night long, and in the morning Maya looked out her window at a sparkling white world. School was closed for the day! She pulled on her boots, her puffy coat and her striped hat, grabbed her sled and hurried outside with her little brother, Owen.

Next door, Mr. Garcia stood on his front step. He leaned on his cane and looked at the deep snow on his sidewalk. His daughter was coming to take him to lunch, and her car would park at the end of his long, snowy path.

Maya looked at her sled. Then she looked at Mr. Garcia. "Owen," she whispered, "let's go get the shovels." The two of them dug and scraped for almost an hour, until their arms ached and their cheeks turned pink from the cold. At last, there was a clear path all the way from Mr. Garcia's front door to the street.

Mr. Garcia walked carefully down the path, tapping his cane on the ground. "Thank you both," he said. "You saved my lunch!" When his daughter's car pulled up, he waved good-bye from the window. Then Maya and Owen finally took out their sled.

Later that afternoon, there was a knock on their door. Mr. Garcia's daughter stood on the step with a box. Inside were two cups of hot cocoa and a bag of cookies. A note said, "For the best neighbors on the street."

stories.title: The Paper Bridge
paragraphs: Ms. Patel held up a single sheet of paper. "Today," she said, "each of you will build a bridge out of one piece of paper. It has to cross the gap between two stacks of books. Then we will see how many pennies it can hold."

Tomás laid his paper flat across the gap. It looked like a bridge, but when he set one penny in the middle, the paper sagged and the penny slid to the floor. Across the room, his friend Jada's bridge drooped the same way. Tomás frowned and picked up his penny.

Then Tomás remembered something. At home, his little sister liked to fold paper into fans. When the paper was folded back and forth, it was much harder to bend. Tomás got a new sheet. He folded it into tight pleats, back and forth, like a fan. Then he laid it across the books.

He put one penny on top. It stayed. He added another, and another. The class began to count out loud. "Twenty-one, twenty-two, twenty-three!" Finally, at thirty-four pennies, the bridge bent and the pile of coins slid off with a clatter.

Ms. Patel smiled. "Tomás found a way to make paper stronger without adding anything to it," she said. "Engineers use the same idea when they build real bridges and roofs." Jada was already folding her own new sheet.

stories.title: The Rainy-Day Show
paragraphs: Rain drummed on the windows all Saturday morning. Lucas and his sister, Rosie, had planned to go to the zoo with Grandma, but now the trip was off. Lucas flopped onto the couch. "There's nothing to do," he groaned.

Rosie looked around the living room. She saw an old cardboard box, a pile of socks with no partners and a jar of buttons. Her eyes lit up. "We can't go to the zoo," she said, "so let's bring the zoo here!"

They cut a big window in the side of the box and hung a towel over the top for a curtain. Then they turned the lonely socks into puppets. A gray sock became an elephant with a long trunk. A yellow sock with brown buttons became a giraffe. Lucas made a lion with a mane of orange yarn.

At three o'clock, they lined up chairs and made a ticket for Grandma. She sat in the front row with a bowl of popcorn. The elephant told jokes, the giraffe sang a song, and the lion roared so loudly that Grandma spilled her popcorn. She laughed until she had to wipe her eyes.

When the show was over, Grandma clapped and clapped. Lucas looked out the window. The rain had stopped, and the sun was peeking through the clouds. "Do you want to go to the zoo now?" Grandma asked. Lucas thought for a moment. "Maybe tomorrow," he said. "I think the lion needs to practice his roar."

stories.title: Abuelo's Secret
paragraphs: Every Sunday, Diego's grandfather, Abuelo, made pancakes. They were tall, fluffy and golden. This Sunday, Abuelo was visiting his sister in another town, so Diego decided to make the pancakes himself. Mom said she would help with the hot stove.

Diego found Abuelo's recipe card in a drawer. He mixed flour, sugar, baking powder, eggs and milk in a big bowl. He wanted the batter to be perfect, so he stirred and stirred until his arm was tired and there was not a single lump.

Mom poured the batter into the pan. The pancakes sizzled, but they did not puff up. They came out flat and chewy, like rubber circles. Diego stared at his plate. "These don't look anything like Abuelo's," he said.

That night, Diego called Abuelo on the phone and told him what happened. Abuelo chuckled. "Did you stir it a lot?" he asked. "Yes! Until it was smooth," said Diego. "Ah," said Abuelo. "That is my secret. Stir only until the flour is wet. A few lumps are good. Too much stirring makes pancakes tough."

The next Sunday, Abuelo was home again. This time, Diego stirred the batter only ten times and left the lumps alone. The pancakes rose high in the pan. Abuelo took a bite and gave a thumbs-up. "Now," he said, "you know my secret too."

stories.title: A House for Wrens
paragraphs: Lily wanted birds in her backyard. She had seen a little brown bird hopping along the fence and singing a loud, bubbly song. Her mom said it was a house wren. "Wrens like to nest in small boxes," Mom said. "Maybe we can build one."

On Saturday, they worked in the garage. Mom cut the wood, and Lily sanded the edges until they were smooth. Together they nailed the pieces into a box with a slanted roof. Lily painted it light green. Then Mom drilled a round hole in the front. It was small, only a little wider than a quarter.
"Why is the hole so tiny?" Lily asked. "Won't the birds get stuck?" Mom smiled. "Wrens are very small, so they can squeeze right in. Bigger birds can't fit through. That keeps the wrens' eggs safe."

They hung the birdhouse on a post near the garden. For two weeks, nothing happened. Lily checked every morning before school. Then one day she saw a wren carrying a twig in its beak. It flew to the hole and popped inside. Soon it came back out for another twig, and another.
By June, Lily could hear tiny peeping sounds coming from the box. She kept her distance and watched from the porch with her binoculars. "Mom," she whispered, "we made a home for a whole family."

stories.title: Life in a Beehive
paragraphs: A honeybee hive is like a busy city. A single hive can be home to thousands of bees, and each bee has a job to do. The longest bee in the hive is the queen. Her job is to lay eggs, sometimes more than a thousand in one day.

Most of the bees in a hive are worker bees. Young workers stay inside. They clean the hive, feed the babies and build little wax rooms called cells. Older workers become guards at the door, or they fly outside to find flowers.

When a worker bee finds a good patch of flowers, she flies back to the hive and does a special dance. She wiggles and turns in a pattern. The dance tells the other bees which way to fly and how far to go. Soon many bees are heading to the same flowers.

Bees drink a sweet juice from flowers called nectar. Back at the hive, they put the nectar into the wax cells. Then they fan it with their wings to dry it out. Slowly, the nectar turns into thick, sticky honey. The bees eat the honey in winter, when there are no flowers.

While bees visit flowers, a yellow dust called pollen sticks to their fuzzy bodies. They carry it from flower to flower. This helps plants make seeds and fruit. Many of the apples, berries and pumpkins we eat grow because bees helped them.

stories.title: The Monarch's Long Trip
paragraphs: Every fall, millions of orange and black butterflies begin a long trip. They are called monarch butterflies. Many of them start in Canada and the northern United States. They fly south for weeks. Some fly more than two thousand miles. They go all the way to the mountains of Mexico.

In Mexico, the monarchs gather in forests of tall fir trees. So many butterflies land on the branches that the trees look orange. They hang in big bunches, like orange leaves. They rest there all winter in the cool mountain air.
In spring, the monarchs fly north again. But they do not make the whole trip back. Along the way, they lay eggs. Their children and grandchildren finish the trip north.

Monarchs lay their eggs on just one kind of plant. It is called milkweed. When the caterpillars hatch, milkweed is the only food they eat. Milkweed makes the caterpillars taste bad to birds. The grown butterflies taste bad, too. Their bright orange wings are like a warning sign. The sign says, "Don't eat me!"
Today there is less milkweed than there used to be. People can help by planting milkweed in gardens and schoolyards. Then the monarchs will have more places to lay their eggs.

stories.title: The Clever Octopus
paragraphs: An octopus is a sea animal with a soft body and eight long arms. Each arm is covered with round suckers. The suckers can grab and hold things. They can even taste what they touch! An octopus has no bones at all.

Because it has no bones, an octopus can squeeze into very small spaces. The only hard part of its body is its beak. It uses the beak to bite its food. If the beak fits through a hole, the rest of the octopus can follow. An octopus can slip into a crack in a rock to hide.

An octopus also has clever ways to stay safe. It can change the color of its skin in less than a second. It can turn bumpy like a rock or smooth like sand. When a hungry fish swims by, the octopus seems to disappear. If that does not work, it can squirt a cloud of dark ink and zoom away.

Octopuses are very smart. Scientists have watched them solve puzzles and find their way through mazes. In some aquariums, octopuses have learned to twist the lids off jars to get the food inside. Some octopuses even carry coconut shells around and hide inside them.
